# 2. A physical shear excursion with an exact magnetic average

The magnetic averaging is implemented with ordinary smooth velocity excursions, not impulses.

Let
\[
r(z)=16z^2(1-z)^2,\qquad 0\le z\le1.
\]
Then
\[
r(0)=r(1)=r'(0)=r'(1)=0,
\qquad
\int_0^1r(z)^2\,dz=\frac{128}{315}.                              \tag{2.1}
\]

For one fundamental shear \(F=e_i s(x_j)\), an impulse sign \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), amplitude \(a>0\), and duration \(h\), prescribe the carrier
\[
w(t)=\frac{\sigma a}{h}r'(t/h)F.
\]
Its integrated displacement is
\[
g(t)=\sigma a\,r(t/h).
\]
The carrier starts and ends at zero, and its induction propagator starts and ends at the identity.

Since \(\mathcal B(F,F)=0\), its ideal mechanical force is
\[
f_w=w_t-\nu\Delta w
=\sigma\left[
 \frac{a}{h^2}r''(t/h)
 +\frac{\nu\kappa^2a}{h}r'(t/h)
 \right]F.                                                       \tag{2.2}
\]
This has time degree at most three. Replacing the occurrence of \(\kappa^2\) in the coefficient by a paid rational approximation creates an additive momentum error.

Write \(B=\mathcal M_{g(t)}b\), using the induction propagator from the question. Its linear equation becomes
\[
b_t=\rho\mathcal M_{g(t)}^{-1}\Delta\mathcal M_{g(t)}b.            \tag{2.3}
\]

Use the four excursions consisting of the two signs and the sine/cosine pair for a fixed orientation. The supplied conjugation identity, integrated using (2.1), gives the average
\[
\Delta+\frac{64\kappa^2a^2}{315}\partial_{ii}.
\]
Use the three cyclic orientations
\[
(i,j)=(1,2),(2,3),(3,1).
\]
The average over the twelve excursions is exactly
\[
\overline A
=\rho\lambda(a)\Delta,\qquad
\lambda(a)=1+\frac{64\kappa^2a^2}{945}.                           \tag{2.4}
\]
For \(a\ge1\), convenient coarse bounds are
\[
2a^2\le\lambda(a)\le6a^2.                                        \tag{2.5}
\]

The principal coefficient of every operator in (2.3) is scalar on vector components and uniformly elliptic. Its inverse ellipticity and all required spatial coefficient bounds are polynomial in \(1+a\). Crucially, they do **not** depend on \(h^{-1}\).

The next step turns this average into an operator-norm contraction.
